newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Battle for skies begins as Korea air show ends.
newsitem.headline: Battle for skies begins as Korea air show ends.

text.p: U.S. aerospace companies attending the first Seoul Air Show found themselves in a dogfight with Western European and Russian rivals for South Korea's multi-billion dollar air defence modernisation programme.

The show, which ended Sunday, produced few major contracts, but it was was abuzz with speculation about who would ultimately land a chunk of Seoul's 20 trillion won ($24 billion) plan to buy or build fighter jets, surveillance planes and other defence equipment by 2010.

"The show went better than I expected, especially for a first effort," said one European exhibitor preparing to close his booth as jets roared over the Seoul City Airport to the thrill of thousands of families out for the day.

Among the few deals struck during the show, Samsung Aerospace Industries said it signed a deal with Northrup Grumman to supply parts for Boeing Co.'s 747-500 aircraft. It hoped to win around $200 million in orders.
Samsung also signed an agreement with Pratt & Whitney Canada, a unit of United Technologies Corp., to build engines for the Bell Helicopter 427 light twin-engine helicopter.
Korean Air Lines Co. and Sikorsky Aircraft Corp., a unit of United Technologies Corp, also agreed to jointly invest $400 million over the next six years to develop multi-purpose helicopters.
However, no decision is expected to be made until at least 1997, or even later, on South Korea's main purchases.

Top contenders for South Korea's next generation fighter jet programme, known as the FX project, are the U.S. Air Force's F-15E developed by McDonnell Douglas Corp., France's Dassault Aviation's Rafale, Russia's Sukhoi Su-35 and the Eurofighter 2000.
South Korea plans to buy 120 planes under the FX programme. These will join the 120 F-16 planes Seoul is acquiring through its Korea Fighter Programme, launched in the late 1980s.
The programme is designed to reinforce the nation's superiority over North Korea's MiG fighters.
More than 200 exhibitors from 21 nations attended the show, said Cha Chong-yol, the organising committee's co-director.
There was no government funding for the show, which was paid for by revenue from exhibitor fees, advertising and entry charges, he said.
"A show like this is important for our country because the development of the aerospace industry will be the basis of Korean advancement into the ranks of the truly developed nations," Cha said.
The Seoul Air Show will be held biennally, with the next show scheduled for October 1998, organisers said.
